citations.quote: A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure ([[def-measure]]) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and let
$\varepsilon \in F$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is a natural number
$n \ge 1$ such that

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of $F$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) and
$1/(n \cdot 1_F)$ is its multiplicative inverse ([[def-field]]). As is standard
we abbreviate $n \cdot 1_F$ to $n$ and write the conclusion $1/n < \varepsilon$.

This is the **reciprocal form** of the Archimedean property.
[[thm-of-archimedean]] on its own delivers only the assertion that the canonical
naturals are cofinal, $x < n \cdot 1_F$; the form actually used in analysis, that
the reciprocals of the naturals get below every positive bound, is the statement
above, and it is recorded separately so that no proof has to reconstruct the
inversion step in passing.

derivations.claim: If $M=0$, then $f=0$ pointwise and both integrals vanish. Suppose $M>0$, put $g=f+M$, and fix an integer $n\ge1$. With $\Delta=2M/n$, define $A_k=\{x:g(x)\ge k\Delta\}$ for $1\le k\le n$ and $s_n=\Delta\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbf1_{A_k}$. The sets are measurable, $s_n$ is nonnegative simple, and the equally spaced lower approximation gives $0\le g-s_n\le\Delta$ pointwise.

By [F3]–[F5], $\int s_n\,dP=\Delta\sum_{k=1}^nP(A_k)$ and likewise for $Q$, so $|\int s_n\,dP-\int s_n\,dQ|\le n\Delta\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}=2M\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}$. Also $0\le\int(g-s_n)\,dP\le\Delta$ and $0\le\int(g-s_n)\,dQ\le\Delta$, because $g-s_n\le\Delta$ and both measures have mass one. The triangle inequality therefore gives $|\int g\,dP-\int g\,dQ|\le2M\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}+4M/n$.

Given any $\eta>0$, choose $n$ by [F7] with $1/n<\eta$; step 2.1 holds for every $n$, so its remainder tends to zero and $|\int g\,dP-\int g\,dQ|\le2M\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}$. Also $|f|\le M$, so [F1], [F3]–[F5] give $\int|f|\,dP\le M$ and $\int|f|\,dQ\le M$; hence $f$ is integrable under both measures by [F6]. The constant $M$ has integral $M$ under each probability measure, so linearity [F6] gives $\int f\,dP-\int f\,dQ=\int g\,dP-\int g\,dQ$. This proves the claim.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) constructed in this
library ([[def-real-numbers]]) and carrying its order ([[def-real-order]]).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
[[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]] records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]] proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
([[def-max-min]], [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space as in [[def-probability-measure]], let $\theta\in\mathbb R$ be a fixed target, and let $m\in\mathbb N\cup\{0\}$. Take $r_1,\ldots,r_m$ and $\widetilde r$ to be real random variables on this space, meaning measurable maps $(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ as in [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]. Set $r_0(\omega):=\theta$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$. Deterministic values are included by using a one-point probability space. The reference chain $r_0,r_1,\ldots,r_m$ must put every quantity on the same scale and state which ideal analysis stage each transition represents. Define the signed stage errors pointwise by
$$e_j:=r_j-r_{j-1}\qquad(1\le j\le m)$$
and the final numerical error
$$e_{\mathrm{fp}}:=\widetilde r-r_m.$$

Each error is measurable because finite sums and differences of measurable real-valued functions are measurable ([[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]]).

When the stages are present, $e_1$ may record data-sampling error, a later transition may record a bootstrap or permutation approximation, a discretized target may record numerical-model bias, and a finite simulation may record computation-randomization error. The labels describe the declared adjacent references; they do not by themselves assert that errors are independent, centered, unbiased, or even random. If a stage is absent, omit it or set its two adjacent references equal. If no floating-point computation is involved, set $\widetilde r=r_m$.

For a probability statement about these errors, the required joint probability law and any conditioning convention must also be specified. For example, fixing the observed data and varying independent randomizations concerns computation error conditional on those data; it does not include variation across new data samples. A deterministic quadrature rule has no replicate-based error estimate unless an actual randomization is added. Any numerical roundoff bound must state its arithmetic and normal-range hypotheses.

Let $\theta=r_0,r_1,\ldots,r_m,\widetilde r$ be the finite scalar reference chain and returned value of [[def-statistical-and-computational-error-ledger]], with $m\ge0$. Then, pointwise,
$$\widetilde r-\theta=\sum_{j=1}^{m}(r_j-r_{j-1})+(\widetilde r-r_m),$$
and consequently
$$|\widetilde r-\theta|\le\sum_{j=1}^{m}|r_j-r_{j-1}|+|\widetilde r-r_m|.$$
The sum is empty when $m=0$. No independence, unbiasedness, or distributional assumption is needed.

Let $E_1,\ldots,E_m$ be square-integrable real random variables on one probability space, where $m\ge1$. Write $b_j=\mathbb E E_j$. Then
$$\mathbb E\left[\left(\sum_{j=1}^{m}E_j\right)^2\right]=\left(\sum_{j=1}^{m}b_j\right)^2+\sum_{j=1}^{m}\operatorname{Var}(E_j)+2\sum_{1\le j<k\le m}\operatorname{Cov}(E_j,E_k).$$
The correction to the sum of component variances is exactly $(\sum_j b_j)^2+2\sum_{j<k}\operatorname{Cov}(E_j,E_k)$. Thus the mean square equals the sum of component variances exactly when this combined correction is zero. In particular, if the total bias is zero, pairwise independence suffices.

derivations.claim: We prove by induction on $m$ that $d(T_0,T_m)\le\sum_{j=1}^{m}d(T_{j-1},T_j)$. For $m=0$ both sides are zero; for $m=1$ this is equality. If it holds through $m$, then the triangle inequality [F1] gives $d(T_0,T_{m+1})\le d(T_0,T_m)+d(T_m,T_{m+1})\le\sum_{j=1}^{m+1}d(T_{j-1},T_j)$.

Apply the triangle inequality once more to $T_0,T_m,\widehat T$ and then step 1.1 to bound $d(T_0,\widehat T)$ by the displayed sum. For a scalar chain, [F2] specifies the same-scale adjacent errors and [F3] gives their exact signed telescope; when the terms are square-integrable, [F4] explains why squaring them retains bias and covariance terms rather than giving an automatic variance sum.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix a measurable parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, a prior probability measure $\Pi_0$ on it, observed data $x$, and an explicitly supplied $\mathcal T$-measurable likelihood version $\ell_x:\Theta\to[0,\infty)$. Define the evidence
$$Z_x:=\int_\Theta \ell_x\,d\Pi_0.$$
When $0<Z_x<\infty$, the **exact inferential target** is the probability measure
$$\Pi_x(A):=\frac{1}{Z_x}\int_A\ell_x\,d\Pi_0\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
The measure is well-defined by the indefinite-integral construction
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]. This is a fixed-data definition: [[def-likelihood-density]] selects versions separately for fixed observations and supplies no common parameter-indexed measurable version. The required version and its measurability must therefore be stated; no posterior is assigned here when the evidence is zero or infinite.

For approximation accounting, declare a metric space $(\mathcal M,d)$ and a finite chain of elements $T_0,T_1,\ldots,T_m,\widehat T\in\mathcal M$, where $m\ge1$ and $T_1=\Pi_x$ whenever the exact target is included. The first distance $d(T_0,T_1)$ is the declared reference-to-target discrepancy; later adjacent distances and $d(T_m,\widehat T)$ are approximation and computation discrepancies on the same metric scale. For probability measures on a common measurable space, total variation may be used with the event-supremum convention of [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]. For scalar random quantities on one probability space, the statistical and computational stages are the same-scale signed differences defined in [[def-statistical-and-computational-error-ledger]]. This notation does not assert independence, unbiasedness, convergence, or that any numerical method attains a global optimum.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).
The dominating measure is part of the specified setup. This condition adds no
measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

In a parametric model $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
two parameter values $\theta,\eta\in\Theta$ are **observationally
equivalent**, written $\theta\sim\eta$, if and only if
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta,
$$
that is, $P_\theta(A)=P_\eta(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). Equivalent parameter values therefore
give exactly the same sampling law. No distinctness of $\theta$ and $\eta$ is
required.

For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be compact, Lebesgue measurable,
and of positive Lebesgue measure. Let $a:K\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable with
$\int_K a\,d\lambda_d<\infty$. Let $h:K\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and have
a unique maximizer $\hat\theta$ in the interior of $K$. Assume $a$ is
continuous at $\hat\theta$ with $0<a(\hat\theta)<\infty$. Suppose $h$ is $C^3$ on an
open neighborhood $U\subseteq K$ of $\hat\theta$, and put
$H:=-D^2h(\hat\theta)$ using the Hessian convention of
[[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]. Assume $H$ is symmetric positive
definite in the sense of
[[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]].
For $x\in\mathbb R^d$ and $r>0$, write
$B(x,r):=\{\theta\in\mathbb R^d:\|\theta-x\|_2<r\}$ and
$\overline B(x,r):=\{\theta\in\mathbb R^d:\|\theta-x\|_2\le r\}$.
Assume there are
$r_0,c,r_1,\eta>0$ such that $\overline B(\hat\theta,r_0)\subseteq U\cap K$,
$$
h(\theta)\le h(\hat\theta)-c\|\theta-\hat\theta\|_2^2
\quad(\theta\in\overline B(\hat\theta,r_0)),
$$
and
$$
h(\theta)\le h(\hat\theta)-\eta
\quad(\theta\in K\setminus B(\hat\theta,r_1)).
$$
All integrals are the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].
For $I_n:=\int_K a(\theta)e^{nh(\theta)}\,d\lambda_d(\theta)$, as the
positive integer $n\to\infty$,
$$
I_n\sim a(\hat\theta)e^{nh(\hat\theta)}\left(\frac{2\pi}{n}\right)^{d/2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\det H}},
$$
where $u_n\sim v_n$ means $u_n/v_n\to1$. No relative $O(n^{-1})$ remainder
is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and let $H\in M_d(\mathbb R)$,
the square-matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]],
be symmetric positive definite in the sense of
[[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]]. Let $\lambda_d$ denote
the Lebesgue measure of
[[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]. Interpret the
displayed integral as the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].
$$
\int_{\mathbb R^d}\exp\!\left(-\frac12 u^{\mathsf T}Hu\right)\,d\lambda_d(u)
=\frac{(2\pi)^{d/2}}{\sqrt{\det H}}.
$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $Y$ be a subspace of a topological space $X$. Then

$$\mathcal B(Y)=\mathcal B(X)|_Y.$$

The Cauchy-sequence reals $\mathbb{R}_C$ have the **least-upper-bound property**:
every nonempty $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}_C$ that is bounded above has a least upper
bound $\sup S \in \mathbb{R}_C$. Hence, together with [[thm-reals-ordered-field]],
$\mathbb{R}_C$ is a **complete ordered field** ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

The relation of [[def-real-order]] is well defined and makes $\mathbb{R}$
([[thm-reals-field]]) a totally ordered field.

Every complete ordered field $F$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) is Archimedean:
for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
([[def-ordered-field]]). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field. For $a, b \ge 0$:

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Fix a measurable parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, a prior probability measure $\Pi_0$ on it, observed data $x$, and an explicitly supplied $\mathcal T$-measurable likelihood version $\ell_x:\Theta\to[0,\infty)$. Define the evidence
$$Z_x:=\int_\Theta \ell_x\,d\Pi_0.$$
When $0<Z_x<\infty$, the **exact inferential target** is the probability measure
$$\Pi_x(A):=\frac{1}{Z_x}\int_A\ell_x\,d\Pi_0\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
The measure is well-defined by the indefinite-integral construction
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]. This is a fixed-data definition: [[def-likelihood-density]] selects versions separately for fixed observations and supplies no common parameter-indexed measurable version. The required version and its measurability must therefore be stated; no posterior is assigned here when the evidence is zero or infinite.

For approximation accounting, declare a metric space $(\mathcal M,d)$ and a finite chain of elements $T_0,T_1,\ldots,T_m,\widehat T\in\mathcal M$, where $m\ge1$ and $T_1=\Pi_x$ whenever the exact target is included. The first distance $d(T_0,T_1)$ is the declared reference-to-target discrepancy; later adjacent distances and $d(T_m,\widehat T)$ are approximation and computation discrepancies on the same metric scale. For probability measures on a common measurable space, total variation may be used with the event-supremum convention of [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]. For scalar random quantities on one probability space, the statistical and computational stages are the same-scale signed differences defined in [[def-statistical-and-computational-error-ledger]]. This notation does not assert independence, unbiasedness, convergence, or that any numerical method attains a global optimum.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. Let $\gamma:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$ be measurable and suppose
$$Z:=\int_\Omega\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty).$$
Define the normalized target density $\pi:=\gamma/Z$. Then $\int\pi\,d\mu=1$. For a measurable probability density $q\ge0$, write $q\ll_\mu\pi$ to mean $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{\pi=0\}$. This is a support condition on the two densities. It ensures that the induced probability measures $Q:=q\,\mu$ and $\Pi:=\pi\,\mu$ have $Q\ll\Pi$.

The normalization follows from positive-scalar homogeneity of the nonnegative integral:
$$\int\pi\,d\mu=Z^{-1}\int\gamma\,d\mu=1.$$
The induced density set functions are measures by [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]. Their total masses are one: $Q(\Omega)=1$ by the probability-density hypothesis on $q$, and $\Pi(\Omega)=1$ by the preceding calculation. To verify the absolute-continuity claim, let $A\in\mathcal A$ satisfy $\Pi(A)=0$. Then $\int_A\pi\,d\mu=0$, so the zero-integral criterion gives $\pi=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $A$. The support condition then gives $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $A$, and hence $Q(A)=0$. The homogeneity and zero-integral criteria used here are [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]] and [[thm-nonnegative-integral-zero-iff-zero-almost-everywhere]].

Call $q$ **admissible** when $q\ll_\mu\pi$ and
$$\int_\Omega q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty.$$
Use $0\log0=0$, and set the products $q\log\gamma$ and $q\log q$ equal to zero on $\{q=0\}$. On the set where $q>0$, admissibility implies $\gamma>0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere. Define the finite real number
$$\operatorname{ELBO}(q):=\int_\Omega q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu.$$
A **variational family** is a nonempty set of admissible densities. A maximizing member need not exist.

For a finite integer $m\ge1$, let $\Omega=\prod_{j=1}^m\Omega_j$, let each $(\Omega_j,\mathcal A_j,\mu_j)$ be sigma-finite, and let $\mu=\bigotimes_{j=1}^m\mu_j$. A **mean-field density** is a product $q(z)=\prod_{j=1}^m q_j(z_j)$ of probability densities $q_j$; it belongs to the admissible mean-field family only when the product satisfies the support and integrability conditions above. Tonelli gives $\int q\,d\mu=1$. The product form alone does not guarantee support or finite ELBO.

In a dominated Bayesian model, a posterior interpretation is available only with the model hypotheses and on fibers with finite positive evidence, as in [[thm-bayes-formula-for-dominated-kernels]] and [[thm-conditional-density-formula]]. In particular, [[def-likelihood-density]] supplies separate likelihood versions but does not assert joint measurability in parameter and data. Supply the single jointly measurable density $\gamma$ explicitly before using Tonelli or a posterior-kernel formula. No quotient is formed at zero or infinite normalizer.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.
Assume AC. The function $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ is positive and Borel measurable on $\mathbb R$, with Lebesgue integral one.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$, $\sigma\ge0$, and a real random variable
$X$ with law $N(m,\sigma^2)$,
$$E[X]=m,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the product measure $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ and the Euclidean Lebesgue
measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ agree on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

derivations.claim: Let $\rho=1/2$, so $\beta=1-\rho^2=3/4$, and write $\phi(t)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-t^2/2}$. By [A1], the AC and Countable Choice premises of [F3], [F7] and [F8] hold. All displayed densities and their polynomial moment integrands are Borel and product-measurable by continuity and [F8]; [F7] supplies the sigma-finite factors for Tonelli and Fubini and identifies their Borel product integrals with the displayed plane Lebesgue integrals. Direct algebra gives $\gamma(x,y)=\phi(x)g_{\rho x,\beta}(y)=\phi(y)g_{\rho y,\beta}(x)$. Each inner Gaussian density has mass one by [F3], so Tonelli [F4] proves that $\gamma$ has mass one and both marginals $\phi$. By [F3] and density integration [F6], the marginal means are zero and second moments are one. Since $|xy|\le(x^2+y^2)/2$, the cross moment is absolutely integrable. Fubini [F5], [F6] and the mean of $g_{\rho x,\beta}$ in [F3] give $E[XY]=\int x\phi(x)\rho x\,dx=\rho$. Thus the target has marginal variances $1$ and covariance $1/2$. With likelihood one the evidence is $1$, so [F1] identifies $\gamma$ as the exact target.

For $m_j\in\mathbb R$ and $v_j>0$, [F3] supplies the normalized Lebesgue densities $g_{m_j,v_j}$ and their means $m_j$ and variances $v_j$. Tonelli [F4] gives total mass one for $q$. The logarithms of $\gamma$ and $q$ are quadratic; the finite second moments and $|xy|\le(x^2+y^2)/2$ make their absolute values integrable under $q$. Both densities are everywhere positive, so $q$ is admissible by [F2]. Fubini [F5] and [F6] give $E_q[X^2]=m_1^2+v_1$, $E_q[Y^2]=m_2^2+v_2$, and $E_q[XY]=m_1m_2$.

One has $\log\gamma=-\log(2\pi\sqrt\beta)-(x^2-xy+y^2)/(2\beta)$ and $-E_{g_{m_j,v_j}}\log g_{m_j,v_j}=\tfrac12\log(2\pi v_j)+\tfrac12$, using the mean and variance in step 1.2. Substituting these expressions and the second moments from step 1.2 into [F2] yields $\operatorname{ELBO}(q)=C-\frac{m_1^2-m_1m_2+m_2^2+v_1+v_2}{2\beta}+\frac12\log v_1+\frac12\log v_2$, where $C$ is independent of $(m_1,m_2,v_1,v_2)$. The mean quadratic equals $(m_1-\rho m_2)^2+\beta m_2^2$, so its unique minimum and the ELBO-maximizing means are $m_1=m_2=0$.

For either variance the variable part is $r(v)=-v/(2\beta)+\tfrac12\log v$, with derivative $r'(v)=(\beta-v)/(2\beta v)$. It is positive on $(0,\beta)$ and negative on $(\beta,\infty)$, so the unique maximum is $v=\beta=3/4$. The target variance is $1$ and covariance is $1/2$ by step 1.1, whereas the optimizing independent factors have variance $3/4$ and covariance $0$ by step 1.2. Thus the unique ELBO optimizer differs from the exact target.

[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]. This is a fixed-data definition: [[def-likelihood-density]] selects versions separately for fixed observations and supplies no common parameter-indexed measurable version. The required version and its measurability must therefore be stated; no posterior is assigned here when the evidence is zero or infinite.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment and let $S:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a statistic, meaning a measurable map to its declared Borel target as in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]], where $d\ge1$ is finite. Expectations are Lebesgue integrals under $P_\theta$ as in [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]], and variances and covariances use centered second moments as in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. For every $\theta\in\Theta$, assume
$$\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[\|S\|_2^2\right]<\infty,\qquad \|x\|_2^2:=\sum_{j=1}^d x_j^2. $$
The **binding mean** and **summary covariance** are the pointwise-defined quantities
$$b_j(\theta):=\mathbb E_\theta[S_j],\qquad \Sigma_{jk}(\theta):=\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[(S_j-b_j(\theta))(S_k-b_k(\theta))\right]\quad(1\le j,k\le d). $$
Each covariance entry is finite since $2|uv|\le u^2+v^2$ and the coordinates are square-integrable. The matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite because for $a\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$a^T\Sigma(\theta)a=\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[(a^T(S-b(\theta)))^2\right]\ge0. $$
No measurability or continuity of $\theta\mapsto b(\theta)$ or $\theta\mapsto\Sigma(\theta)$ follows from these pointwise definitions.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). If $\Sigma(\theta)$ is positive definite, the **ideal Gaussian synthetic likelihood** for observed data $y\in\mathcal X$ is the Gaussian density evaluated at its summary, as supplied by [[def-multivariate-normal-law]] and [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]],
$$g_{\mathrm{SL}}(y\mid\theta):=\varphi_d\!\left(S(y);b(\theta),\Sigma(\theta)\right)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma(\theta))^{-1/2}\exp\!\left[-\tfrac12(S(y)-b(\theta))^T\Sigma(\theta)^{-1}(S(y)-b(\theta))\right]. $$
Here $\varphi_d(\,\cdot\,;m,\Sigma)$ is the Lebesgue density of $N_d(m,\Sigma)$. If $\Sigma(\theta)$ is singular, this positive-definite-covariance density is not defined by this item.

For $m\ge2$ IID simulated summaries $S_1,\ldots,S_m$ from $P_\theta\circ S^{-1}$, set
$$\bar S_m:=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m S_i,\qquad \widehat\Sigma_m:=(m-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m(S_i-\bar S_m)(S_i-\bar S_m)^T. $$
The **finite-simulation plug-in synthetic likelihood** is the random quantity
$$\widehat g_{\mathrm{SL},m}(y\mid\theta):=\varphi_d(S(y);\bar S_m,\widehat\Sigma_m). $$
when $\widehat\Sigma_m$ is positive definite, and is **unavailable** otherwise. The finite plug-in quantity is a function of simulated summaries; it is not defined as an unbiased estimator of the ideal Gaussian density.

The exact experiment’s likelihood density, when the experiment is dominated as in [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]] and given a pointwise density as in [[def-likelihood-density]], and this Gaussian summary approximation are different objects. No optimizer or optimizer convergence property is included.

For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

In a parametric model $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
two parameter values $\theta,\eta\in\Theta$ are **observationally
equivalent**, written $\theta\sim\eta$, if and only if
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta,
$$
that is, $P_\theta(A)=P_\eta(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). Equivalent parameter values therefore
give exactly the same sampling law. No distinctness of $\theta$ and $\eta$ is
required.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment and let $S:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a statistic, meaning a measurable map to its declared Borel target as in [[def-statistic-and-estimator]], where $d\ge1$ is finite. Expectations are Lebesgue integrals under $P_\theta$ as in [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]], and variances and covariances use centered second moments as in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. For every $\theta\in\Theta$, assume
$$\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[\|S\|_2^2\right]<\infty,\qquad \|x\|_2^2:=\sum_{j=1}^d x_j^2. $$
The **binding mean** and **summary covariance** are the pointwise-defined quantities
$$b_j(\theta):=\mathbb E_\theta[S_j],\qquad \Sigma_{jk}(\theta):=\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[(S_j-b_j(\theta))(S_k-b_k(\theta))\right]\quad(1\le j,k\le d). $$
Each covariance entry is finite since $2|uv|\le u^2+v^2$ and the coordinates are square-integrable. The matrix is symmetric and positive semidefinite because for $a\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$a^T\Sigma(\theta)a=\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[(a^T(S-b(\theta)))^2\right]\ge0. $$
No measurability or continuity of $\theta\mapsto b(\theta)$ or $\theta\mapsto\Sigma(\theta)$ follows from these pointwise definitions.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). If $\Sigma(\theta)$ is positive definite, the **ideal Gaussian synthetic likelihood** for observed data $y\in\mathcal X$ is the Gaussian density evaluated at its summary, as supplied by [[def-multivariate-normal-law]] and [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]],
$$g_{\mathrm{SL}}(y\mid\theta):=\varphi_d\!\left(S(y);b(\theta),\Sigma(\theta)\right)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma(\theta))^{-1/2}\exp\!\left[-\tfrac12(S(y)-b(\theta))^T\Sigma(\theta)^{-1}(S(y)-b(\theta))\right]. $$
Here $\varphi_d(\,\cdot\,;m,\Sigma)$ is the Lebesgue density of $N_d(m,\Sigma)$. If $\Sigma(\theta)$ is singular, this positive-definite-covariance density is not defined by this item.

For $m\ge2$ IID simulated summaries $S_1,\ldots,S_m$ from $P_\theta\circ S^{-1}$, set
$$\bar S_m:=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m S_i,\qquad \widehat\Sigma_m:=(m-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m(S_i-\bar S_m)(S_i-\bar S_m)^T. $$
The **finite-simulation plug-in synthetic likelihood** is the random quantity
$$\widehat g_{\mathrm{SL},m}(y\mid\theta):=\varphi_d(S(y);\bar S_m,\widehat\Sigma_m). $$
when $\widehat\Sigma_m$ is positive definite, and is **unavailable** otherwise. The finite plug-in quantity is a function of simulated summaries; it is not defined as an unbiased estimator of the ideal Gaussian density.

The exact experiment’s likelihood density, when the experiment is dominated as in [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]] and given a pointwise density as in [[def-likelihood-density]], and this Gaussian summary approximation are different objects. The latter density-selection interface assumes AC and does not assert a common exceptional null set across an arbitrary parameter set; the present definition adds no parameter-indexed measurability. This definition makes no claim that the actual summary law is Gaussian, that $g_{\mathrm{SL}}$ equals an exact likelihood, or that it yields posterior calibration, consistency, a Bernstein–von Mises theorem, or coverage. No optimizer or optimizer convergence property is included.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

The finite identity summary is measurable because the source and target carry their stated power-set and Borel sigma-algebras.

Under $P_0$, $E[S]=(0+1+2+3)/4=3/2$ and $E[S^2]=(0+1+4+9)/4=7/2$. Under $P_1$, the corresponding weighted sums are $(9+6+21)/24=3/2$ and $(9+12+63)/24=7/2$. Thus both variances equal $7/2-(3/2)^2=5/4>0$, so the one-dimensional covariance is positive definite and the ideal Gaussian synthetic likelihood is defined by [F2], [F4].

The two posterior measures differ on event $\{1\}$ by $|3/5-1/2|=1/10$, so their total-variation distance is at least $1/10$ by [F5]. Thus matching the first two moments does not remove this posterior target bias.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be standard Borel spaces. Let $\Pi$ be a prior probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and let $K$ be a probability kernel from $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, as in [[def-bayesian-model-as-prior-and-sampling-kernel]]. Let $S:\mathsf Y\to\mathbb R^d$ be a measurable statistic for a fixed integer $d\ge1$, and fix an observed summary $s_0\in\mathbb R^d$. The Euclidean norm is $\|x\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d x_j^2)^{1/2}$.

Under the prior-simulator joint law, first draw $\theta\sim\Pi$ and then $Y\sim K(\theta,\cdot)$. The summary-predictive probability measure $M$ on $\Theta\times\mathbb R^d$ is the law of $(\theta,S(Y))$; on measurable rectangles it is
$$M(A\times C)=\int_A K(\theta,S^{-1}(C))\,\Pi(d\theta).$$
The prior and simulator define a joint law by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]], and the change-of-variables formula identifies $M$ as the law after applying $S$ ([[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]]).

For $\epsilon\ge0$, define the closed tolerance ball
$$B_\epsilon(s_0)=\{s\in\mathbb R^d:\|s-s_0\|_2\le\epsilon\}.$$
Its prior-predictive acceptance probability is
$$p_\epsilon(s_0):=M(\Theta\times B_\epsilon(s_0))\in[0,1].$$
Only when $p_\epsilon(s_0)>0$ define the indicator ABC target by
$$\Pi_\epsilon(A\mid s_0):=\frac{M(A\times B_\epsilon(s_0))}{p_\epsilon(s_0)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
This is exactly the conditional law of $\theta$ under the augmented event $S(Y)\in B_\epsilon(s_0)$. The denominator is finite because $M$ is a probability, and no quotient is assigned when the event has probability zero. This target is the posterior given a tolerance event, not in general the full-data posterior or the posterior given the exact summary.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

In a parametric model $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
two parameter values $\theta,\eta\in\Theta$ are **observationally
equivalent**, written $\theta\sim\eta$, if and only if
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta,
$$
that is, $P_\theta(A)=P_\eta(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). Equivalent parameter values therefore
give exactly the same sampling law. No distinctness of $\theta$ and $\eta$ is
required.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

Fix a measurable parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, a prior probability measure $\Pi_0$ on it, observed data $x$, and an explicitly supplied $\mathcal T$-measurable likelihood version $\ell_x:\Theta\to[0,\infty)$. Define the evidence
$$Z_x:=\int_\Theta \ell_x\,d\Pi_0.$$
When $0<Z_x<\infty$, the **exact inferential target** is the probability measure
$$\Pi_x(A):=\frac{1}{Z_x}\int_A\ell_x\,d\Pi_0\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
The measure is well-defined by the indefinite-integral construction
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]. This is a fixed-data definition: [[def-likelihood-density]] selects versions separately for fixed observations and supplies no common parameter-indexed measurable version. The required version and its measurability must therefore be stated; no posterior is assigned here when the evidence is zero or infinite.

For approximation accounting, declare a metric space $(\mathcal M,d)$ and a finite chain of elements $T_0,T_1,\ldots,T_m,\widehat T\in\mathcal M$, where $m\ge1$ and $T_1=\Pi_x$ whenever the exact target is included. The first distance $d(T_0,T_1)$ is the declared reference-to-target discrepancy; later adjacent distances and $d(T_m,\widehat T)$ are approximation and computation discrepancies on the same metric scale. For probability measures on a common measurable space, total variation may be used with the event-supremum convention of [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]. For scalar random quantities on one probability space, the statistical and computational stages are the same-scale signed differences defined in [[def-statistical-and-computational-error-ledger]]. This notation does not assert independence, unbiasedness, convergence, or that any numerical method attains a global optimum.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) constructed in this
library ([[def-real-numbers]]) and carrying its order ([[def-real-order]]).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
[[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]] records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]] proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
([[def-max-min]], [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

$(X,d)$ is **complete** if every Cauchy sequence in $(X,d)$
([[def-cauchy-in-metric]]) converges to a point of $X$
([[def-metric-convergence]]).

A subset $A \subseteq X$ is called **complete** when the metric subspace
$(A, d_A)$ is complete ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]); as always, the
metric is part of the data, and $d_A$ is the restriction of $d$ to $A \times A$.

**The limit is unique when it exists**, since limits in a metric space are unique
([[lem-metric-limits-unique]]), so a complete space assigns to each of its Cauchy
sequences one point and not a set of points.

**Completeness is a property of the pair $(X,d)$, not of $X$ and not of the
topology of $d$.** Both quantifiers in the definition are about the metric: the
Cauchy condition is stated with distances, and so is convergence. Two metrics on
the same set can have the same open sets while exactly one of them is complete,
which is the content of [[fs-completeness-is-a-topological-property]] and its
witness. Read the word *complete* as an abbreviation for *complete with respect
to this metric*, always.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

derivations.claim: Put the discrete metric on $\Theta$ and $\mathsf Y$. A Cauchy sequence is eventually constant because its tail has pairwise distances below $1/2$; each finite space is separable since the whole finite set is a countable dense subset. Every subset is open, so the Borel sigma-algebra is the power set. Thus both are standard Borel by [F5]. The real target is standard Borel by [F5].
The event $A=\{(z,w):z=0\}$ has probabilities $P_0(A)=1$ and $P_1(A)=0$. Thus the two full-data laws are not observationally equivalent, and the identity parameter is identifiable by [F3].
The full-data likelihood at $y=(0,0)$ is $1/2$ under $\theta=0$ and $0$ under $\theta=1$. Its prior evidence is $(1/2)(1/2)+(1/2)0=1/4$, so [F4] gives exact posterior $\Pi_y=\delta_0$.

For each $\theta$, exactly two pairs $(z,w)$ have $z=\theta$, each with mass $1/2$, so $P_\theta$ is a probability law; because the parameter sigma-algebra is also the power set, the displayed family is a probability kernel. The map $S$ is nonconstant, since $S(0,0)=0$ and $S(0,1)=1$, and it is measurable because every subset of the finite source is measurable.

The summary law is Bernoulli$(1/2)$ under each parameter. The zero-tolerance ball in $\mathbb R$ centered at $S(y)=0$ is $\{0\}$, and each parameter has acceptance probability $1/2$, so prior-predictive acceptance is $1/2>0$. Conditioning the equal prior on this event leaves $\Pi_{\mathrm{ABC},0}\{\theta=0\}=\frac{(1/2)(1/2)}{1/2}=1/2$ by [F1].

On event $\{\theta=0\}$ the exact posterior gives mass $1$ and the zero-tolerance ABC target gives mass $1/2$. By [F6], their total-variation distance is at least $1/2$. The full model is identifiable, but the nonconstant summary has parameter-independent law and its ABC target remains the prior.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be standard Borel spaces. Let $\Pi$ be a prior probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and let $K$ be a probability kernel from $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$, as in [[def-bayesian-model-as-prior-and-sampling-kernel]]. Let $S:\mathsf Y\to\mathbb R^d$ be a measurable statistic for a fixed integer $d\ge1$, and fix an observed summary $s_0\in\mathbb R^d$. The Euclidean norm is $\|x\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d x_j^2)^{1/2}$.

Under the prior-simulator joint law, first draw $\theta\sim\Pi$ and then $Y\sim K(\theta,\cdot)$. The summary-predictive probability measure $M$ on $\Theta\times\mathbb R^d$ is the law of $(\theta,S(Y))$; on measurable rectangles it is
$$M(A\times C)=\int_A K(\theta,S^{-1}(C))\,\Pi(d\theta).$$
The prior and simulator define a joint law by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]], and the change-of-variables formula identifies $M$ as the law after applying $S$ ([[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]]).

For $\epsilon\ge0$, define the closed tolerance ball
$$B_\epsilon(s_0)=\{s\in\mathbb R^d:\|s-s_0\|_2\le\epsilon\}.$$
Its prior-predictive acceptance probability is
$$p_\epsilon(s_0):=M(\Theta\times B_\epsilon(s_0))\in[0,1].$$
Only when $p_\epsilon(s_0)>0$ define the indicator ABC target by
$$\Pi_\epsilon(A\mid s_0):=\frac{M(A\times B_\epsilon(s_0))}{p_\epsilon(s_0)}\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
This is exactly the conditional law of $\theta$ under the augmented event $S(Y)\in B_\epsilon(s_0)$. The denominator is finite because $M$ is a probability, and no quotient is assigned when the event has probability zero. This target is the posterior given a tolerance event, not in general the full-data posterior or the posterior given the exact summary.

Use the model and notation of [[def-approximate-bayesian-computation]] and the procedure [[alg-abc-rejection]]. Let $B=B_\epsilon(s_0)$ and $p=M(\Theta\times B)>0$. Suppose the proposals and simulator outputs form an IID sequence $(\Theta_j,Y_j)_{j\ge1}$ with the prior-simulator joint law. Then the first accepted index
$$N:=\inf\{j\ge1:S(Y_j)\in B\}$$
is finite almost surely, and the accepted parameter has law
$$\mathbb P(\Theta_N\in A)=\frac{M(A\times B)}{p}=\Pi_\epsilon(A\mid s_0)\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
Thus the accepted parameter has exactly the tolerance-conditioned target law. This statement does not identify that target with the full-data posterior or assert an expected proposal count.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) constructed in this
library ([[def-real-numbers]]) and carrying its order ([[def-real-order]]).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
[[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]] records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]] proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
([[def-max-min]], [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

$(X,d)$ is **complete** if every Cauchy sequence in $(X,d)$
([[def-cauchy-in-metric]]) converges to a point of $X$
([[def-metric-convergence]]).

A subset $A \subseteq X$ is called **complete** when the metric subspace
$(A, d_A)$ is complete ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]); as always, the
metric is part of the data, and $d_A$ is the restriction of $d$ to $A \times A$.

**The limit is unique when it exists**, since limits in a metric space are unique
([[lem-metric-limits-unique]]), so a complete space assigns to each of its Cauchy
sequences one point and not a set of points.

**Completeness is a property of the pair $(X,d)$, not of $X$ and not of the
topology of $d$.** Both quantifiers in the definition are about the metric: the
Cauchy condition is stated with distances, and so is convergence. Two metrics on
the same set can have the same open sets while exactly one of them is complete,
which is the content of [[fs-completeness-is-a-topological-property]] and its
witness. Read the word *complete* as an abbreviation for *complete with respect
to this metric*, always.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Fix a measurable parameter space $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, a prior probability measure $\Pi_0$ on it, observed data $x$, and an explicitly supplied $\mathcal T$-measurable likelihood version $\ell_x:\Theta\to[0,\infty)$. Define the evidence
$$Z_x:=\int_\Theta \ell_x\,d\Pi_0.$$
When $0<Z_x<\infty$, the **exact inferential target** is the probability measure
$$\Pi_x(A):=\frac{1}{Z_x}\int_A\ell_x\,d\Pi_0\qquad(A\in\mathcal T).$$
The measure is well-defined by the indefinite-integral construction
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]]. This is a fixed-data definition: [[def-likelihood-density]] selects versions separately for fixed observations and supplies no common parameter-indexed measurable version. The required version and its measurability must therefore be stated; no posterior is assigned here when the evidence is zero or infinite.

For approximation accounting, declare a metric space $(\mathcal M,d)$ and a finite chain of elements $T_0,T_1,\ldots,T_m,\widehat T\in\mathcal M$, where $m\ge1$ and $T_1=\Pi_x$ whenever the exact target is included. The first distance $d(T_0,T_1)$ is the declared reference-to-target discrepancy; later adjacent distances and $d(T_m,\widehat T)$ are approximation and computation discrepancies on the same metric scale. For probability measures on a common measurable space, total variation may be used with the event-supremum convention of [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]. For scalar random quantities on one probability space, the statistical and computational stages are the same-scale signed differences defined in [[def-statistical-and-computational-error-ledger]]. This notation does not assert independence, unbiasedness, convergence, or that any numerical method attains a global optimum.

Let $\mu$ and $\nu$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
$(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **total variation
distance** is

$$\lVert\mu-\nu\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}\bigl|\mu(A)-\nu(A)\bigr| .$$

For every event $A$ the difference $\mu(A)-\nu(A)$ is a real number in
$[-1,1]$, because both measures have total mass one; hence the set being
maximized is a nonempty subset of $[0,1]$ and the supremum lies in $[0,1]$.
The empty event and the whole space give the values $0$ and
$|\mu(E)-\nu(E)|=0$, so the distance is zero when $\mu=\nu$, and it is symmetric
in $\mu$ and $\nu$. This convention carries no factor $1/2$ in the supremum;
it is therefore not the total variation norm of the signed measure $\mu-\nu$,
which is twice the quantity above when that signed measure is considered on a
measurable space where the decomposition is attained. On a countable state
space with its power-set sigma-algebra the supremum equals the half-$\ell^1$
sum $\tfrac12\sum_{x\in E}|\mu(\{x\})-\nu(\{x\})|$; that identity is proved in
[[lem-total-variation-half-l1-formula-on-a-countable-space]], not assumed here.

derivations.claim: Each row sums to one and has nonnegative entries, so it defines a probability kernel on the finite parameter and data spaces. Under the discrete metric a Cauchy sequence is eventually constant (take tail distances below $1/2$); each finite set is separable and all of its subsets are open. Hence both are standard Borel. The summary map $S$ is measurable to the real Borel sigma-algebra because every preimage is a subset of the finite measurable data space, by [F3].

At observation $1$, the likelihoods are $1/5$ and $4/5$, so the exact posterior mass at $\theta=1$ is $(4/5)/(1/5+4/5)=4/5$ by [F4]. The closed $\epsilon$-ball around $1$ is $\{1/2,1\}$. Its conditional probabilities are $P_0(B)=3/5+1/5=4/5$ and $P_1(B)=1/10+4/5=9/10$. Therefore the prior-predictive acceptance probability is $\frac12(4/5+9/10)=17/20>0$.
Conditioning the prior-simulator law on this ball gives ABC mass at $\theta=1$ equal to $\frac{(1/2)(9/10)}{17/20}=9/17$ by [F1]. The exact and ABC posterior masses differ by $|4/5-9/17|=23/85$.

Event $\{\theta=1\}$ shows that the total-variation distance is at least $23/85$ by [F5]. If the proposal-simulator pairs $(\Theta_j,Y_j)$ are IID under the prior-kernel joint law, [F2] identifies this ABC target as the accepted-parameter law; the finite calculations make no additional convergence or efficiency claim.
